summary.text: The expansion of the universe is the increase in distance between gravitationally unbound parts of the observable universe with time.
It is an intrinsic expansion, so it does not mean that the universe expands into anything or that space exists outside it.
To any observer, all but the nearest galaxies move away at speeds that are, on average, proportional to their distance from the observer.

items.prompt: Very distant galaxies are receding faster than light travels, yet relativity is not broken. Why?

options.label: The speed limit applies to local reference frames, not to distant recession
Light speeds up in empty space to stay ahead of them
Their speed is measured wrongly and is really lower
Relativity applies only to objects inside our galaxy

items.explain: Objects cannot move faster than light with respect to local reference frames, but that limit does not restrict the recession rates of cosmologically distant objects.

items.prompt: A child asks what the universe is expanding into. What is the best answer?

options.label: Into a huge empty space that surrounds the universe
Into a wall of matter that sits at the universe's edge
Nothing: the expansion is intrinsic and needs no space outside
Into a second universe that is slowly being pushed back

items.explain: The expansion is intrinsic, so it does not mean the universe expands into anything or that space exists outside it.

items.prompt: Matter in the universe attracts other matter by gravity. Why has the expansion not been stopped by it?

options.label: Gravity only works on objects that are close together
The density is too low for gravity to prevent continued expansion
Gravity pushes outward on matter at great distances
The expansion is much too fast for gravity to matter at all

items.explain: The universe's contents are flying apart, and their gravity slows the expansion but their density is too low to prevent it.

items.prompt: The scale factor tracks the average separation between galaxies and is set to a = 1 today. What value did it have long ago?

options.label: A value below 1, because separations were smaller
A value above 1, because the universe was larger
Exactly 1, since it is a fixed constant
A value of zero, because there were no galaxies yet

items.explain: The scale factor is proportional to average separation and is smaller in the past and larger in the future.

items.prompt: Expansion began with a sudden burst and then slowed. What happened about 4 billion years ago?

options.label: It stopped and began to contract
It sped up suddenly by a huge factor
It slowed to a crawl and then held steady
It began to gradually speed up again, and still is

items.explain: After slowing, expansion began to gradually expand more quickly around 9.8 billion years after the Big Bang (4 billion years ago) and is still doing so.

items.prompt: Why don't the very nearest galaxies follow the pattern of moving away in proportion to distance?

options.label: They are too small to feel any expansion at all
They sit at the center of the universe
Gravity binds them to each other
They are carried along by the galaxies behind them

items.explain: All but the nearest galaxies move away; the nearest ones are bound to each other by gravity.

beats.title: Everything Moving Apart

beats.prompt: You measure two distant galaxies. One is twice as far from you as the other. How do their speeds of moving away compare, on average?
beats.explain: To any observer, galaxies move away at speeds proportional to their distance, on average.

choices.label: The farther one moves away about twice as fast
The nearer one moves away faster
choices.feedback: That has it backwards: speeds are proportional to distance, so farther means faster.

choices.label: Both move away at the same speed
choices.feedback: It is tempting to think speed is a property of each galaxy, but speed grows in proportion to distance.

right.label: Used Einstein's equations to show expansion

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: The speed-of-light limit applies to local reference frames.
Distant galaxies can recede at rates that limit does not cover.
So a galaxy receding faster than light breaks relativity.
So the limit and the expansion can both hold.

paragraphs.heading: Distances that grow
paragraphs.text: The expansion of the universe means that, as time passes, the distances between parts of the observable universe that are not held together by gravity get larger. The expansion is built into space itself. It does not mean the universe is spreading into something, or that there is space outside it. The idea is hard to explain, and it has led to several misconceptions.

paragraphs.heading: What any observer sees
paragraphs.text: Wherever you stand in the universe, all but the closest galaxies seem to be moving away from you. On average, the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes, in proportion to its distance. The nearest galaxies are the exception because gravity binds them together. Nothing can travel faster than light, but that limit only applies locally, so it does not cap how fast very distant objects can recede.

paragraphs.heading: Found in the 1920s
paragraphs.text: Both theory and observation uncovered the expansion in the 1920s. Between 1912 and 1914 Vesto Slipher found that light from remote galaxies was redshifted, which was later read as a sign they are moving away from Earth. In 1922 Alexander Friedmann used Einstein's equations to show in theory that the universe is expanding. In 1927 Georges Lemaître used data from Slipher and Hubble to propose a straight-line link between a galaxy's distance and its speed of recession, and Edwin Hubble firmly established that link in 1929.

paragraphs.heading: Fast, slow, then fast again
paragraphs.text: The standard Lambda-CDM model says the expansion rate has changed over time, depending on what the universe contains. In the earliest stage, called inflation, the universe suddenly stretched at least 10²⁶ times over along each direction. After that the expansion slowed a great deal. Then, about 4 billion years ago, it began to speed up gradually, and it is still doing so. To explain this recent speed-up, physicists have proposed dark energy.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the size of it
paragraphs.text: Cosmologists track the expansion with a number called the scale factor, written a, which grows in step with the average spacing between objects such as galaxies. By convention a = 1 today, so it was smaller in the past and will be larger in the future. Running the clock backward in some models reaches a moment when the scale factor was zero, which current cosmology places 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years ago.

paragraphs.heading: A tug of war
paragraphs.text: One way to picture the expansion is that the universe's contents started out flying apart. The gravity of all the matter and radiation slowly holds the expansion back, but it is too thinly spread to stop it. On top of that, recent evidence suggests dark energy is now making the expansion speed up. If the expansion goes on forever, the scale factor will grow without limit, though in principle the universe could also stop and begin to shrink.
